content: Pitavastatin is the most recently introduced statin available on the market. The specific effects of pitavastatin on blood lipid levels, depending on the dose, have not been fully established. The primary goal of this research was to measure the impact of different doses of pitavastatin on surrogate markers of cardiovascular health, including LDL cholesterol, total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, and triglycerides, in individuals both with and without cardiovascular disease. Additionally, the study aimed to compare the effects of pitavastatin on these markers with those of other statins. A secondary objective was to assess the frequency of treatment discontinuation due to adverse effects at various doses of pitavastatin. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, Embase, the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, and ClinicalTrials.gov, up to March 2019. The search was not restricted by language. Authors of relevant studies were also contacted to identify additional published or unpublished data. The inclusion criteria for the analysis were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and controlled before-and-after studies that evaluated the dose-response relationship of fixed doses of pitavastatin on blood lipid levels over a treatment period of three to 12 weeks. Participants of any age, with or without cardiovascular disease, were included. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of studies and extracted data. Data from RCTs and controlled before-and-after studies were analyzed using Review Manager 5. Information on withdrawals due to adverse effects (WDAE) was specifically collected from the RCTs. The quality of the included studies was evaluated using the Cochrane 'Risk of Bias' tool, which assessed potential biases related to allocation, blinding, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and other sources. A total of 47 studies, including five RCTs and 42 before-and-after studies, were included in the analysis, involving 5,436 participants. The participants ranged in age and included individuals with and without cardiovascular disease. The treatment duration ranged from three to 12 weeks. The analysis of dose-response data for pitavastatin doses ranging from 1 mg to 16 mg demonstrated a strong linear relationship between dose and reductions in blood total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, and triglycerides. However, there was no dose-dependent effect on HDL cholesterol, which increased by an average of 4% across all doses. Pitavastatin at doses of 1 mg/day to 16 mg/day reduced LDL cholesterol by 33.3% to 54.7%, total cholesterol by 23.3% to 39.0%, and triglycerides by 13.0% to 28.1%. For every doubling of the dose, LDL cholesterol decreased by 5.35% (95% CI: 3.32 to 7.38), total cholesterol decreased by 3.93% (95% CI: 2.35 to 5.50), and triglycerides decreased by 3.76% (95% CI: 1.03 to 6.48). The certainty of evidence for these effects was rated as high. When compared to other statins in terms of LDL cholesterol reduction, pitavastatin was found to be approximately six times more potent than atorvastatin, 1.7 times more potent than rosuvastatin, 77 times more potent than fluvastatin, and 3.3 times less potent than cerivastatin. Regarding safety, in the placebo group, no participants withdrew due to adverse effects out of 109 subjects. Across all doses of pitavastatin, three participants withdrew due to adverse effects out of 262 subjects. In conclusion, pitavastatin effectively lowers total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, and triglycerides in a dose-dependent linear manner. Based on its LDL cholesterol-lowering potency, pitavastatin is significantly more potent than atorvastatin, rosuvastatin, and fluvastatin, but less potent than cerivastatin. However, there was insufficient data to draw definitive conclusions about the risk of withdrawal due to adverse effects associated with pitavastatin.
